item.title: The Motorola Moto G Play (2026) is now just $160, making it a solid budget pick
item.itunes:title: The Motorola Moto G Play (2026) is now just $160, making it a solid budget pick
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Since budget phones started adopting high-refresh-rate displays, Motorola has quietly been pushing solid entry-level devices that don't feel cheap. The Motorola Moto G Play (2026) is now available on Woot for $160, which is 36% off its usual retail price of $250.

A solid entry point for folks who want a reliable daily driver without the midrange price tag. You will find a side-mounted fingerprint sensor for quick unlocking, and the water-repellent design adds peace of mind if you get caught in a downpour.

It might not be winning any benchmark races, but it packs a few features that make it stand out in the crowded budget category.

What's great about the Motorola Moto G Play​​​​​​​?

You get a 6.7-inch IPS LCD screen with a 120Hz refresh rate and Corning Gorilla Glass 3 protection. Under the hood, it runs on the MediaTek Dimensity 6300 chipset paired with 4GB of RAM and 64GB of internal storage.

If you need more room for apps and photos, a dedicated microSD slot lets you expand that space. The phone weighs just 202 grams, so it won't feel heavy in your pocket during long commutes. The battery is easily the star of the show here.

The 5,200mAh cell will easily last a full day of heavy use, and while 18W charging isn't the fastest option on the market, it is perfectly fine for a budget phone. Active use benchmarks show it can stretch to nearly 17 hours on a single charge.

That kind of endurance means you can leave the charger at home without worrying about running out by the end of the day. It also runs Android 16 out of the box, which means you get a clean, near-stock software experience right away.

The camera setup is simple but functional. It features a single 32 MP rear sensor that handles HDR and panorama shots well enough for social media. You get an 8 MP front camera for video calls and selfies. It lacks a telephoto lens, but at this price point, you shouldn't expect one anyway.

The stereo speakers with Dolby Atmos support add a nice touch for media consumption, and the 3.5mm headphone jack is still present. This phone is a bargain and is best suited for everyday tasks like messaging, browsing, and light app use.

You can grab the Motorola Moto G Play (2026) for $160 from Woot if you're quick.

item.title: Claude Code's creator says better prompts need just 3 things, so I tested his approach
item.itunes:title: Claude Code's creator says better prompts need just 3 things, so I tested his approach
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
We've successfully reached the stage where every other person has an opinion on how you should be prompting AI. In the same week, you'll hear one person tell you to feed as much context as you possibly can into a prompt, be vague, and let the LLM figure out the details on its own. Then, you'll come across someone else telling you to do the exact opposite: keep your prompts short, be ridiculously specific about what you want, and leave absolutely nothing up to the AI's interpretation.

Sure enough, both sides will swear their approach is the secret to getting better results. This is why I think the best tips come from the people actually building these models and the tools powered by them. After all, who better to tell you how to get the most out of an AI tool than someone who played a role in creating it?

That's exactly why a recent post from Boris Cherny, the creator of Claude Code, caught my attention. Rather than sharing some shiny new, elaborate prompting framework or a ridiculously long template you need to follow, he says a good prompt just needs three things.

Boris Cherny says there's no secret to prompting

Three tips, no magic formula

Cherny frequently shares his Claude Code setup tips over on his X account, and a post he shared on October 6, 2026, caught quite a bit of attention. In the post, he shared an interactive website he'd built using Claude to accompany an episode of the Acquired podcast about Home Depot. Interestingly, it wasn't the website itself that got people talking. Instead, it was the prompt he'd used to create it.

Once he shared the prompt, users were surprised by just how simple and conversational it was. There were no elaborate instructions, complicated prompting frameworks, or special tricks involved. He was essentially talking to Claude the way you'd talk to a coworker, which led quite a few people to realize they'd been prompting their AI tools in a similar way all along.

The reactions eventually prompted Cherny to elaborate on his approach to prompting, and that's when he explained that there's really no secret to it. According to him, a good prompt comes down to just three things.

First up, your prompt should clearly communicate what you want it to do. This is fairly self-explanatory, but it essentially means being clear about what you're trying to accomplish rather than leaving the AI to guess what you have in mind. You don't necessarily need to write an entire paragraph explaining every little detail, but the model should have a good understanding of what you're asking it to do and what you expect the final result to look like.

Something Anthropic's been pushing a lot lately is giving users more control over how much time and computational effort a model spends working through a task, which is referred to as effort. The idea is pretty straightforward: not every task requires the same amount of thinking. You wouldn't necessarily want Claude to spend several minutes reasoning through a simple question, but for something considerably more complicated, giving it more room to think could make a difference. That's essentially what Cherny's second tip boils down to: communicate exactly how much effort you want the AI to put into the task.

Finally, another tip that Cherny has shared in practically all of his Claude Code setup tip articles is giving the tool a way to verify its own work. Rather than simply trusting that the AI has done what you asked it to do correctly, give it a way to check its output. For example, if you're asking Claude Code to build an application, you could ask it to run tests to make sure everything works as intended. The idea is to give the model a clear way to determine whether it's actually accomplished what you asked it to do, rather than just assuming it has.

Cherny's own prompt is an almost perfect example of his advice

He practices (almost) what he preaches

While I could demonstrate Cherny's advice with a prompt I've written myself, I think there's no better example than the very prompt that started this entire conversation in the first place. After all, if we're taking prompting advice from the creator of Claude Code, we might as well look at how he puts his own advice into practice.

The latest acquired Home Depot episode is really amazing. I want you to make an artifact that narrates the entire episode. Make it beautiful and interactive and focus on communicating the nugggets of business wisdom throughout the episode. Make it really good, use lots of tokens and iterate till you're proud of it. Maybe add watercolor illustrations and historical photos throughout, aim for New Yorker or nytimes data viz vibes but better. I think you can use OpenCV for water color images

Let's start with the first tip: clearly communicating what you want the AI to do. Cherny begins his prompt by asking Claude to create an artifact that narrates the entire Home Depot episode. He then gives it a few more details about what he has in mind. He wants the artifact to be beautiful, interactive, and focused on communicating the business lessons from the episode. He even gives Claude some creative direction, suggesting watercolor illustrations, historical photographs, and a visual style inspired by The New Yorker or The New York Times.

What's interesting is that he doesn't tell Claude exactly how to build the artifact. He explains what he wants the final result to look like and leaves the finer details up to the model. The second tip is even easier to spot. Cherny explicitly tells Claude to "use lots of tokens" and keep iterating until it's proud of the result. He's essentially telling the model that he wants it to put considerable effort into the task rather than rushing through it.

Now, the third tip is where things get a little interesting. While Cherny does ask Claude to keep iterating until it's satisfied with the result, he doesn't actually give it a concrete way to verify its work. There are no instructions to run tests or check the final artifact against a specific set of requirements. Instead, he's relying on Claude to evaluate and improve the quality of its own output.

Claude Code's real power comes from the tweaks nobody wants to talk about

Claude Code gets better when you stop chasing flashy workflows and start tightening the boring setup details.

5
By  Jeff Butts

So, while his prompt clearly demonstrates the first two principles, the third is a little less explicit. I think that's especially worth pointing out, because it shows that even Cherny doesn't necessarily treat these three tips as a rigid formula that every prompt needs to follow.

After testing his approach out over the past few days, I've realized that there's a lot of truth to what Cherny is saying. Rather than spending ages trying to craft the perfect prompt or following some elaborate framework I came across online, I've been focusing on clearly communicating what I want, how much effort I expect the AI to put in, and how it should check its work. So far, I've found that this simple approach works surprisingly well, regardless of which AI model I'm using.

The problem with prompting advice is that it doesn't age well

Prompting advice has a surprisingly short shelf life

To be completely fair, when I said that the best prompting tips come from the people actually building these AI models and tools, I didn't mean that everyone else's advice is necessarily wrong. Sure, the LinkedIn prompt engineering gurus might not have all that many credentials to back up their advice, but that doesn't automatically make their tips any less useful. The problem is that prompting advice has a surprisingly short shelf life, and something that works brilliantly today might not work nearly as well a few months down the line.

If you've been following the pace of these AI companies since the day OpenAI dropped its first model publicly, you might've noticed that they're showing no signs of slowing down. A new model seems to drop practically every other week (or at least that's what it feels like), and the entire point of these releases is to improve upon what came before them. Naturally, that also means the way we interact with these models is constantly changing.

I added one line to my Claude Code prompts, and the difference was night and day

One line is all it took

16
By  Mahnoor Faisal

What worked brilliantly with one model might not necessarily work as well with the next, and prompting advice that was considered gospel just a few months ago might already be outdated. To add to that, every AI provider's LLMs are different. A prompting technique that works wonders with Claude might not necessarily produce the same results with ChatGPT or Gemini, even if you're asking all three models to perform the exact same task.

So, between the constant stream of new model releases and the differences between models from competing AI companies, it's no surprise that everyone's constantly trying to figure out the next big prompting trick.

These three tips aren't just for Claude

While Cherny's advice comes from his experience building and using Claude Code, none of these tips are exclusive to Claude. Whether you're using ChatGPT, Gemini, or a local LLM, clearly communicating what you want, how much effort the task requires, and how the model should verify its work can help you get better results.

Ultimately, these aren't complicated prompting tricks that depend on a specific model or tool, but rather simple principles that can be applied to just about any AI assistant!

item.title: Arc browser is getting the axe as its creator goes all-in on AI with Dia
item.itunes:title: Arc browser is getting the axe as its creator goes all-in on AI with Dia
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • Arc will shut down on December 22nd, 2026; users have several weeks to migrate.
  • The Browser Company will replace Arc with Dia, a new browser built with modern security in mind and a focus on AI.
  • Arc features, including bookmarks, extensions, history, Spaces, Folders, and Tab Groups, will transfer easily to Dia.

The Browser Company has revealed plans to discontinue its flagship Arc browser to make way for a new project called Dia. Arc will shut down on December 22nd, giving users several weeks to move on from the popular productivity-focused browser.

Last May, The Browser Company confirmed that Arc's development would end, but it didn't reveal a specific shutdown date at the time. "We've decided to sunset Arc on December 22, 2026," wrote the company in a recent Twitter post. "That's not an easy sentence to write. We spent years building Arc and celebrating each and every release along the way: we have so much pride and love for what we made alongside the Arc community," writes Arc.

Say goodbye to Arc and hello to Dia

The new browser includes AI features like writing assistance, a morning brief, asking questions about web pages, and more

Credit: The Browser Company

In its blog post, The Browser Company says Dia was "built from the ground up" to meet today's security standards, emphasizing that its "engineering and security teams will focus" on the browser moving forward. Switching to the Dia browser should be seamless for Arc users, since key features like bookmarks, extensions, history, Spaces, Folders, and even Tab Groups can be easily transferred to the new browser.

The shutdown is happening in a few stages. Starting now, you can't create a new Arc account. Next, on November 23rd, on iOS and Android, Browse for Me and "other AI features" will be turned off, and the ability to sign in and sync your tabs will be removed. Then lastly, on December 22nd, Arc won't be accessible on Windows 11 or macOS, and all accounts will be deactivated.

"Thank you for using Arc, for pushing us to make it better, and for building alongside us. The team that made Arc is the same team behind Dia, and some of our most ambitious work is ahead. We'd love for you to be there with us when it lands," writes The Browser Company in the blog post.

The Browser Company claims that Dia has "surpassed Arc benchmarks in stability, speed, and security." It also says all the features you use in Arc are free in Dia, and that the browser's AI integrations are optional. With that in mind, if AI isn't your thing, you should be able to turn the majority of those features off. Dia's AI features include writing assistance, a morning brief, asking questions about web pages, and more.

item.title: I moved away from Ubuntu on bare metal to WSL, and my Windows 11 PC handles my everyday Linux tasks now
item.itunes:title: I moved away from Ubuntu on bare metal to WSL, and my Windows 11 PC handles my everyday Linux tasks now
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Although I’ve been an avid distro-hopper for many years, I always used a dual-boot Ubuntu + Windows 11 setup on my daily driver, and for good reason. After all, virtual machines would not only consume a lot of resources if I tried running them on top of a bloated Windows 11 instance, but I’d also have no means of running graphically demanding applications on a VM.

But after running into deal-breaking problems with my bare-metal setup, I started looking into alternatives for my everyday machine. That’s when I stumbled upon WSL, and it single-handedly replaced my Ubuntu boot drive.

5 reasons I stopped dual-booting Windows and Linux on my PC

It's just not worth the hassle anymore.

55
By  Joe Rice-Jones

WSL doesn’t take up as much space as a bare-metal setup

Nor does it hog as many resources as a conventional VM

Back in the day, I’d keep Windows 11 and Ubuntu partitions on the same SSD, and they worked pretty well for the most part. Unfortunately, I’ve had Windows 11 updates break my Ubuntu bootloader on more than one occasion, even though I’d taken all the precautions to keep both operating systems as separate as possible. Although I was able to use a live USB to fix the broken Ubuntu installation, the whole experience left a bad taste in my mouth.

With the prices of SSDs skyrocketing, buying a second drive just for Ubuntu doesn’t make a lot of sense, especially since WSL works exceedingly well for my Linux projects. Better yet, WSL is light enough that the entire setup, including the WSL engine and the Ubuntu files, occupy less than 15GB of space on my Windows 11 host. And since WSL dynamically expands my Linux virtual disk, I don’t need to worry about splitting the partitions evenly between Ubuntu and Windows 11 as I used to in my dual-boot days.

Switching to virtual machines is a viable alternative, sure, but they tend to be quite demanding on my PC. Worse still, I’d have no way to harness my GPU’s firepower in my AI experiments, even on something as powerful as Hyper-V. WSL, on the other hand, supports GPU acceleration, so I can harness my RTX 3080 Ti for Python experiments. Better yet, I can even edit files stored inside my Windows 11 PC directly from my WSL-based Ubuntu instance.

WSL lets me run full-on Linux applications within Windows 11

And I’m not talking just about CLI apps, either

If you’re wondering, my Ubuntu tasks involve coding tools, automation services, and AI-heavy Python projects – all of which work just as well on WSL as they do on a bare-metal setup. However, attempting to access these Linux files from my Windows 11 instance used to require a bunch of workarounds on my dual-boot setup. Not to mention, I’d have to log out of either OS when I wanted to run experiments on the other.

On a WSL-powered setup, the Windows 11 host would remain accessible even when I’m knee-deep in my Ubuntu experiments. As such, I can just leave my WSL projects running in the background and switch to my multiplayer titles on Windows 11 while the apt package manager installs the necessary packages for my experiments.

Heck, even GUI-laden applications work well on WSL. Sure, I may use CLI tools for the most part, but if I ever need to test GUI tools once I’m done coding them, I can just fire them up like any other app. Plus, good ol’ VS Code has its own WSL integration on Windows 11, which makes switching between my host machine and my Ubuntu dev environment a lot easier than manually cycling between the two operating systems on a bare-metal setup. While we’re on this subject…

Switching distros is fairly simple on WSL, too

I’ve stuck to the Ubuntu flavor on my WSL setup, but I can just as easily tinker with other distributions. Debian, Kali Linux, openSUSE, Fedora, Arch, and AlmaLinux are officially available on WSL, and configuring them is as simple as running wsl --install distro_name. However, the talented Linux community has also created fully-functional WSL instances of NixOS, Gentoo, and other quirky (but highly useful) distros as well.

NixOS on WSL, for example, has the same declarative nature that I’ve grown to love (and at times, hate) during my distro-hopping misadventures, and rolling back changes is as simple on WSL as it is on a bare-metal setup. Better yet, since these distros barely occupy 5-10 GB on my Windows 11 host, I don’t need to mass-delete files just to experiment with a specific distro.

I ditched Docker for WSL containers in my homelab, and here's what failed first

Not a lot, to be honest.

3
By  Anurag Singh

WSL is just that easy to use

When I first heard about WSL, I was worried that I’d have to deal with a long setup process and fix random compatibility errors. However, WSL is surprisingly easy to configure, to the point where you can get the engine and a distro running in well under 30 minutes. I’ve also yet to encounter any performance issues or deal-breaking compatibility problems after years of messing around with wild WSL projects.

If you've been holding out for a display that can keep up with modern frame rates without blowing your budget, the timing is finally right. This Acer Nitro 27" WQHD monitor is now available with a significant discount, making it a compelling way to upgrade your desk setup.

Whether you're pushing through fast-paced shooters or managing a workstation, this monitor delivers the speed and clarity you need without the usual premium markup. Right now, it's sitting at a major low at just $135 at Walmart, which makes it one of the easiest upgrades you can make this year.

At its core, this is a 27-inch IPS panel that delivers a crisp 2560 x 1440 WQHD resolution. The real draw is the up to 200Hz refresh rate paired with a 0.5ms gray-to-gray response time. The zero-frame bezel keeps visual clutter to a minimum for multi-panel setups.

item.title: Docker isn't the hard part of self-hosting, and the part that is gets skipped by almost everyone
item.itunes:title: Docker isn't the hard part of self-hosting, and the part that is gets skipped by almost everyone
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
With modern self-hosting, it's easy to copy a .yaml block, run `docker compose up -d`, and see a slick web dashboard pop up on `localhost:8080`. It makes you feel like a DevOps genius in under five minutes. A week later, your household can't access the service because local IP addresses have changed and your browser yells about insecure HTTP/SSL warnings. Exposing a raw port to the web gets your server hammered by automated port scanners.

Docker has solved application deployment, but it didn't solve networking infrastructure, secure remote access, edge routing, or data lifecycle management. Spinning up a container is the easy part; it's a simple copy and paste. The hard part of self-hosting is building the underlying network, reverse proxying, local DNS, and a disaster-recovery stack around Docker, and skipping it turns your home lab into an unstable, insecure mess.

4 essential Docker containers i run on every new server

A collection of handy containers to manage my workstations

9
By  Ayush Pande

Why do your containers fall apart?

This admin is essential

Many standard Docker tutorials skip critical networking and administration layers, but they cause day-2 infrastructure crises if you haven't implemented them. Out of the box, Docker forces you to manage raw ports like :8080, :9000, :3000, and memorizing IP and port combinations isn't sustainable. Setting up proper split-horizon local DNS via Pi-hole, AdGuard Home, or Unbound to route human-readable domain names like vault.home.arpa locally is the step everyone skips. Setting this up makes accessing your containers significantly easier without you having to manage those raw ports.

Running web services over unencrypted HTTP exposes credentials over local Wi-Fi, so you need to ensure that you set up a reverse proxy and TLS certificate engine. Routing traffic through a reverse proxy like Caddy or Nginx Proxy Manager with automated Let's Encrypt/ACME SSL certificates is a non-negotiable for zero-trust security.

And lastly, mounting a local Docker volume or bind mount to your host SSD feels like a backup, but in reality it's just live data. True data preservation requires automated off-site 3-2-1 backup strategies using tools like Borg Backup, Restic, or Kopia. These handle database dumps before host drive failures occur, so you never have to be at risk of losing all of your data.

What steps should you take?

Be sure you implement these steps whenever you deploy a container

If you want to migrate from a container server that feels like it falls apart and needs constant maintenance to a production home lab, follow these steps. First, build the edge, like your reverse proxy and certificates. This should be step number one. Spin up a dedicated edge router/proxy container, like Caddy, and attach it to an internal Docker network before launching any user-facing apps.

Next, you can implement local split DNS by configuring your local DNS server to rewrite your home domain's wildcards directly to your reverse proxy's IP address. This will allow you to access all of your apps by typing in clean, memorable URLs instead of those messy IP addresses. Instead of having to type in port numbers, you can just type in jellyfin.home.arpa.

If you want some secure remote access without port forwarding, then you have to make sure you lock down your router's firewall and route off-site traffic through a service like Tailscale, WireGuard, or Cloudflare tunnels with strict authentication rules. Tailscale lets you securely connect to your computers, servers, home labs, and NAS devices from anywhere by creating an encrypted mesh network without requiring any public IP addresses, complex firewalls, or manual port forwarding.

And lastly, make sure you're automating off-site 3-2-1 backups. Write cron jobs or deploy dedicated backup containers to snapshot application state, dump database schemas, encrypt volumes, and sync them to off-site cloud or secondary hardware targets.

It's not all peachy

But these issues can be resolved

It's worth noting the issues that you might encounter. For example, Docker's default network isolation might get in your way and create some real-world operational challenges. Docker's internal bridge networks isolate containers by default, making external reverse proxies choke unless you properly design custom Docker networks.

Updating a container image without backing up its backing database volume can also cause failed schema migrations, creating a lot of maintenance debt. Establishing image-pinning policies, like locking to specific version tags instead of `:latest`, can keep production services from breaking silently overnight, so you feel like there's much less maintenance involved.

Docker isn't hard

But it's not as simple as it seems on the surface

Docker made deploying software trivial, but it didn't remove the actual responsibilities of system administration before deploying all of your containers. True self-hosting mastery isn't about running 50 containers; it's about building a robust, secure infrastructure underneath them so they stay online effortlessly. Close Docker Hub, step back from adding new services, and dedicate a weekend to building the reverse proxy, local DNS, and off-site backup layers your home lab actually deserves.

Establishing image-pinning policies, like locking to specific version tags instead of `:latest`, can keep production services from breaking silently overnight, so you feel like there's much less maintenance involved.

Docker isn't hard

But it's not as simple as it seems on the surface

Docker made deploying software trivial, but it didn't remove the actual responsibilities of system administration before deploying all of your containers. True self-hosting mastery isn't about running 50 containers; it's about building a robust, secure infrastructure underneath them so they stay online effortlessly. Close Docker Hub, step back from adding new services, and dedicate a weekend to building the reverse proxy, local DNS, and off-site backup layers your home lab actually deserves.

item.title: Windows already has a screen recorder, OCR, clipboard history, and an antivirus that people still pay third-parties for
item.itunes:title: Windows already has a screen recorder, OCR, clipboard history, and an antivirus that people still pay third-parties for
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Lately, most of the online discourse surrounding Microsoft Windows has been about its shortcomings, the tedious bloat of its services, and AI features that no one wants. I agree with most of the points raised, but the trouble is, a lot of the useful tools Microsoft ships with Windows 11 get lost in the noise.

I've been looking back at how much of my daily workflow runs on tools I got for free the day I installed Windows 11. Most people never find out these tools exist, so they type their problem into Google, reach for the first "sponsored" result, and sign up for a subscription that solves a problem that the OS already did. If you're on any version of Windows 11 and still paying for a screen capture utility, an OCR tool, or any antivirus at all, you're paying twice for the same thing.

I can't imagine my workflow without Snipping Tool

The screenshot app has been getting better all this time

The Snipping Tool has been a part of Microsoft Windows since Windows 7, but it has gotten a lot more capable and a lot more versatile since then. If you've only been using it to screen grab an item or another all this time, there's a chance you've missed a lot of the developments.

The designated screenshot app has turned into three apps at once, and the keyboard shortcut is still the one that most users who have ever used it are familiar with. Win+Shift+S pulls up the capture bar, whereas Win+Shift+R begins a screen recording of any region you draw. Win+Shift+T on the other hand, runs OCR on anything on the screen without going through the screenshot process.

What's gotten better, however, is that every single one of these tools has received some rather impressive quality-of-life improvements. OCR, for example, now features a Quick Redact button alongside it that wipes every email address and phone number out of a screenshot in a single click, which, depending on your workflow, can save you from five minutes to hours of work taking them out yourself.

The screen recorder borrows from the best bit of Clipchamp through Edit in Clipchamp after handoff, where your clip gets passed to the Captions tab and can be transcribed on the spot if necessary. Even the screenshot tool has gotten better, and that's something you'd have noticed if you ever complained about HDR captures looking washed-out or oversaturated, because Snipping Tool now runs a color corrector in the background.

4 reasons I'm still using Snipping Tool instead of the technically better alternatives

There are technically better options out there, but Snipping Tool is perfect for my needs.

2
By  Adam Conway

Clipboard history is the Windows feature I talk about the least

And yet, I probably use the most

One of the most challenging aspects of working (which I believe, is compounded tenfold when you read and write for a living) with texts and links is that Windows only remembers the last thing that was copied to the clipboard, and if you accidentally copy something else, whatever you saved before has been replaced.

I imagine it's something that has sent plenty of users looking for third-party clipboard managers, and that's how utilities like Ditto and CopyQ have a market. Before you reach for third-party alternatives, though, it's worth knowing that Windows has had a perfectly functional alternative built into the OS since Windows 10.

With the combination Win + V, you can find your Clipboard History, which comes up as a searchable panel that keeps track of the last 25 copied items, including text, images, and all the hyperlinks that you lost while going over a dozen different tabs. What's even neat for someone like me who has two Windows 11 PCs is the fact that you can have the clipboard sync across devices, which means I can access copied items on my desktop as I resume work on my laptop.

6 clipboard managers for Windows that will change how you work

The clipboard is more than you might think

11
By  João Carrasqueira

The only antivirus I need is already on Windows 11

It's built in, always on, always free, and literally the best at the moment

The days of a Norton or Avira subscription being the first thing you put on a fresh Windows PC are long behind us, and yet, somehow, half the people I help with their PCs think that Windows' own security is something of a placeholder until they install a real antivirus that they must pay for.

Independent labs have been scoring Microsoft Defender against paid products that do the same job for many years, and the results have been the very same. Microsoft's built-in protection has been decimating its competition in the past couple of years, and there hasn't been a legitimate reason to look at paid alternatives.

In May and June this year, AV-TEST evaluated Microsoft Defender and gave it a perfect 6.0/6.0 score on protection, 5.5/6.0 on performance and 6.0/6.0 on usability, with a total of 17.5 out of 18, which earned it the "Top Product" award. In terms of protection, Defender caught 100% of 0-day malware thrown at it and 100% of prevalent malware reference set. Across 1.2 million legitimate software samples, it only raised a singular false alarm.

15 Windows software tools you’ve never heard of but should be using

Discover 15 hidden gem tools for Windows that boost productivity, enhance privacy, and simplify tasks.

17
By  Pranav Bhardwaj

If you paid for Windows, you paid for all of this already

We've all been in a place where we're desperate for a certain feature or utility, and we're more than happy to just throw our credit cards at paid utilities to make the immediate problems go away. However, the more you know your way around your OS, the more you know what it can do for you, the easier your experience on it will be. With Windows 11, there are a lot of features at your disposal just one-click away, and all the utilities that I mention here have been more than enough to serve me as a power user. As always, it's best first to research first, and swipe your card after.

item.title: Nvidia's next GeForce flagship is rumored to lose half its CUDA cores overnight
item.itunes:title: Nvidia's next GeForce flagship is rumored to lose half its CUDA cores overnight
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
The RTX 5090 is the most powerful gaming GPU ever released, and it comes with 21,760 CUDA cores on its GB202 Blackwell chip, which is just over two times the amount that comes on the RTX 5080. If October's leaks are correct and a 24GB RTX 5080 becomes the best GeForce card that gamers can buy, Nvidia's flagship gaming offering essentially loses half of its compute overnight. Jeff Fisher, Senior VP of everything GeForce at Nvidia, has told Taiwanese media that the 5090 isn't going anywhere, but that doesn't mean much when nobody can actually buy one.

More affordable Nvidia RTX 5080 "Blackwell" graphics card might release on this date

A new leak has revealed the release date of the much-awaited Nvidia RTX 5080 GPU.

3
By  Rahul Naskar

A 24GB RTX 5080 is still half of an RTX 5090

The extra VRAM is nice at the extremes, but not much else changes

The rumored launch of the 24GB variant of the RTX 5080 is expected to carry the "Super" branding that has been dormant since the 40-series GPUs, but this new variant isn't changing anything about the main silicon. The RTX 5080 already uses the full GB203 die, so Nvidia has nothing left to unlock without moving to a cut-down GB202, which is already in short supply. The leaks also describe a power bump, going to a 415W TDP, a 55W increase over the 360W on the standard card.

For those who game at 4K with the graphical fidelity cranked, the memory and power upgrades are meaningful. 16GB already causes trouble in the most demanding games. Indiana Jones and the Great Circle, for example, breaks down at 4K with path tracing on a 16GB card. Even so, a memory upgrade on a card that launched in January 2025 is not a new flagship, and it just means Nvidia would be topping its GeForce lineup with silicon it has been selling for almost two years already.

Realistically, the market has already made this choice, because the 5090 was unattainable for the vast majority of gamers, even those that could afford the $1,999 MSRP price tag. The cheapest RTX 5090 is currently around $8,000 at the time of writing, while the cheapest RTX 5080 is around $1,700. The 5080 has been Nvidia's real top gaming card for awhile now.

The RTX 5080 is the first 80-class GPU in Nvidia's history that couldn't beat the last-gen flagship, and that says a lot

I wouldn't mind calling it the RTX 4080 Ti at this point.

5
By  Hamlin Rozario

The 80-class has been drifting away from the top for three generations

The gap has been getting larger

Two generations ago, the gap looked pretty different: the RTX 3080 had 8,704 CUDA cores to the RTX 3090’s 10,496, or about 83%. Both cards came from the same GA102 die, so the 3090 was essentially a "fuller" version of the 3080, though they were much closer than the cards that came after them.

The RTX 4080 moved to the smaller AD103 die while the 4090 stayed on AD102, and the 4080’s 9,728 cores came to about 59% of the 4090’s 16,384, and that continued with Blackwell. Over three generations, the 80-class cards went from being most of a flagship to being about half of one.

As someone who owns both an RTX 3080 and RTX 5080, I have never felt like either wasn't enough for high-resolution gaming for the titles released around the time of the card. The 3080 was especially an excellent value in retrospect, considering it can still handle many newer games at 4K with Quality upscaling. The 5080 is definitely a meaningful upgrade, providing much better 1% lows over the 3080 when the resolution isn't as high, but with its bigger VRAM buffer and bump in compute helps it be an everyday 4K gaming card without upscaling.

Compared to what the alleged RTX 5080 Super will be, it's hard to tell without having one in-hand, but I haven't come across a game personally where the 16GB capacity was a limiting factor in performance, even with texture quality and filtering maxed.

AMD's RX 9070 XT just beat the RTX 5080

A little undervolting goes a long way.

7
By  Jacob Roach

The GB202 has more profitable places to be

The 5090 turned out to be a much better compute card than a gaming one

GB202 powers both the RTX 5090 and the RTX Pro 6000 Blackwell workstation card. Every GB202 that becomes a GeForce card is one that can’t become a much more expensive Pro card, and it's no secret that even the RTX 5090 is highly sought after for its prowess as a workstation card over a gaming one.

Fisher’s denial addressed end-of-life, not how GB202 chips are allocated, and the popularity of the silicon for the workstation purpose being far more profitable means that the price of the 5090 is not coming down anytime soon. It doesn't mean the leak is true, and Nvidia could simply be struggling to source enough GDDR7 for a 32GB consumer card. Buyers don't care about that, though; if stock doesn't exist for them to buy, the result is the same either way.

5 reasons my RTX 3080 to RTX 5080 upgrade dream is ruined

I hoped the RTX 5080 would replace my RTX 3080, but the dream is dead.

29
By  Tanveer Singh

We'll find out more about the alleged 50-series Super refresh soon enough

CES 2027 should be the next checkpoint for the GeForce brand as a whole. If Nvidia announces a 24GB RTX 5080 there, how it’s positioned matters a lot: if it's the same GB203 with more memory, presented as the best GeForce card you can actually buy, the GB202 is essentially dead for gamers. There are rumors of an "SE" variant of the 5090, which includes a cut-down GB202, but those rumors are unsubstantiated at the time of writing.

The 3080 was especially an excellent value in retrospect, considering it can still handle many newer games at 4K with Quality upscaling. The 5080 is definitely a meaningful upgrade, providing much better 1% lows over the 3080 when the resolution isn't as high, but with its bigger VRAM buffer and bump in compute helps it be an everyday 4K gaming card without upscaling.

Compared to what the alleged RTX 5080 Super will be, it's hard to tell without having one in-hand, but I haven't come across a game personally where the 16GB capacity was a limiting factor in performance, even with texture quality and filtering maxed.

The GB202 has more profitable places to be

The 5090 turned out to be a much better compute card than a gaming one

GB202 powers both the RTX 5090 and the RTX Pro 6000 Blackwell workstation card. Every GB202 that becomes a GeForce card is one that can’t become a much more expensive Pro card, and it's no secret that even the RTX 5090 is highly sought after for its prowess as a workstation card over a gaming one.

Fisher’s denial addressed end-of-life, not how GB202 chips are allocated, and the popularity of the silicon for the workstation purpose being far more profitable means that the price of the 5090 is not coming down anytime soon. It doesn't mean the leak is true, and Nvidia could simply be struggling to source enough GDDR7 for a 32GB consumer card. Buyers don't care about that, though; if stock doesn't exist for them to buy, the result is the same either way.

The cheapest RTX 5090 is currently around $8,000 at the time of writing, while the cheapest RTX 5080 is around $1,700. The 5080 has been Nvidia's real top gaming card for awhile now.
